extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and critics of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic and dramatic works—especially tragedy and epic—covering their definition, constituent parts, plot construction, language, metre, and effects on the audience. Emphasizes principles such as unity, imitation, catharsis, and the hierarchical importance of plot over other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (katharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains each phrase: 'serious' implies elevated subject-matter; 'complete' means having a beginning, middle, and end; 'magnitude' refers to suitable scale; language includes rhythm, harmony, and song introduced in parts; must be enacted (dramatic) rather than narrated; the purpose is to arouse pity and fear and produce catharsis. The definition is central and used to evaluate whether a work is a tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (Mythos / Fable) as primary element
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of incidents of the story (the Plot or Fable) is the most important of the six parts; tragedy is essentially an imitation of action and life, and action (the Plot) is the end and purpose of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must represent action, not merely present character sketches; beginners succeed more easily in diction or character than in plot construction. Powerful attractions of tragedy—peripety (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition)—are plot devices. A strong plot requires causal unity: incidents should follow because of one another (necessary or probable). A play may exist without character but not without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) as secondary element
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is what makes us ascribe moral qualities to agents and is second in importance to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be consistent and appropriate to the action; character reveals moral purpose (what agents seek or avoid). Character must serve the plot; the absence of character is common in some modern plays (a defect). Hamartia (error) may be part of character but need not be a moral vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) – reasoning and ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the power of saying whatever can be said, or what is appropriate to the occasion; it appears when characters prove points or enunciate general truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown in speeches that argue or demonstrate; related to rhetoric and political discourse. Should be distinguished from Character; Thought is about what is said and its appropriateness to situation. Good Thought supports Plot and Character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis) – composition of verse and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction means the composition of the verses—the style and choice of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elaborate diction is required only where there is no action, Character, or Thought to be revealed; where Character or Thought are present, ornate diction can obscure them. Diction must suit metre and occasion; word-choices, metaphors, and linguistic usages should be defensible by custom, punctuation, or metaphorical reading when criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (Melos) / Music
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (song, musical element) is one of the means of imitation and a pleasurable accessory in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music contributes substantially to the pleasure of the drama and is an addition to the elements found in epic poetry. Melody should be integrated appropriately in the parts where song is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) – stage appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (the spectacle or stage-appearance of the actors) is a part of the whole but is least artistic and arises more from the production apparatus than from the poet's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle has great emotional effect but is the least intrinsic to the poet's craft. Over-reliance on gesture or spectacle (overacting) can be criticized as interpreter's, not poet's, failing. Movement should be dignified and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for Unity: each part should subserve the whole, and irrelevancies, however brilliant, should be cast away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy (and good art) requires unity of action; events should be arranged so the whole work reads as a single coherent action with a beginning, middle, and end. Unity is linked to the preference for necessary or probable connections between incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be complete in itself and of a certain magnitude—large enough to be serious and have proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness implies discernible beginning, middle, and end; magnitude concerns suitable scale for the effect (not trivial). Epic differs by allowing greater length; tragedy tends to keep within a single circuit of the sun (unity of time) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Imitation: Means, Objects, Manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic arts differ in three ways: by their means (rhythm, language, harmony), by their objects (types of persons represented: better, worse, or like us), and by the manner (narrative, mixed, or dramatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify and design works: e.g., tragedy and epic both imitate serious actions but differ in metre and form; some arts mix rhythm, melody, and verse (dithyrambic); some use language alone. The choice affects tone, metre, and mode of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (katharsis) – purpose of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy effects the proper purgation (katharsis) of pity and fear by arousing those emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catharsis may derive from ritual origins (Dionysiac purification) and denotes a therapeutic or purgative effect on the community and spectators. This end helps justify certain poetic choices but must be evidenced by the work's ability to arouse and dispose of pity and fear properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity in Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence of events should be either necessary or probable and should 'appear to happen because of one another'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sequences that feel random; prefer causally linked incidents. A likely impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility. Improbabilities that are unavoidable should be placed outside the action or justified by opinion; otherwise they are faults of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot; Use of Peripeteia and Anagnorisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots include Reversal of Fortune (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis); simple plots lack these and are less intricate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia and anagnorisis are powerful devices in tragic plots and often occur together; they derive from ritual patterns and can heighten catharsis. However, not every tragic plot requires recognition or reversal—use according to historical form and desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (error) in the tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical tragic hero falls from high state not through vice or depravity but by some great hamartia—originally an 'error' or 'bad shot'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia should be understood broadly (error, mistake, or flaw) rather than strictly as moral depravity; it's often an intellectual error or misjudgment. Avoid over-precise translations; focus on how the character's mistake generates consequences in the Plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of Action, not of Persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is primarily an imitation of action and life; characters are included for the sake of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing plays, prioritize the sequence and causal structure of actions; Character and Thought should serve to reveal or propel action rather than supplant it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Metre and Form per Genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry is in heroic metre and narrative form; tragedy uses metres suited to speech (iambic) and dramatic form; metre should fit the nature of the imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic is tolerant of strange words and longer narratives; tragedy favors speakable metres. Avoid improbable metre choices (e.g., long epic in medley metres) that create incongruity with genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling the Marvellous and the Improbable
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous and improbable can produce pleasure; a likely impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improbable incidents are necessary, place them outside the action or justify them by opinion; conceal improbabilities with other excellences. Do not include gratuitous improbabilities that could have been made more probable without harming the Plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Contradictions and Technical Incorrectness
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms often allege impossible, improbable, corrupting, contradictory, or technically incorrect elements; such faults should be answered by showing they serve poetry, accord with opinion, or are defensible linguistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiqued for falsity, reply that the poet may portray things as they ought to be or in accordance with opinion; contradictions should be examined for equivocal meanings, punctuation, dialectal usage, or metaphorical senses before condemning the poet. Technical errors tied directly to the art are more culpable than accidental errors of specialized knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Parts of Tragedy (canonical list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has six parts: Plot (Fable), Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, and Melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this canonical list as a checklist for composition and critical evaluation. The list organizes elements by means, manner, and object of imitation; Plot and Character arise from objects, Diction and Melody from means, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and Contextual Evaluation of Deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a word or deed in poetry is morally right, consider the agent, the recipient, the time, the means, and the motive—whether done to attain a greater good or avoid a greater evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation in poetry depends on dramatic context; do not judge isolated actions without considering the circumstances and the character's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Use of Poet's Intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak little in propria persona; excessive intrusion undermines imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing through characters rather than lengthy authorial exposition. Homer is praised for bringing in characters quickly without prolonged poetial preface; avoid overt narratorial presence that breaks dramatic imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific Object Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres represent different types of persons: tragedy typically portrays people better than the average, comedy people worse than average, and some arts depict people like ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subject-matter and character types consistent with genre aims (e.g., tragedy elevates, comedy targets the ridiculous). Understanding this distinction informs tone, diction, and moral distance between audience and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: comparative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy share many elements, but epic differs in narrative form and length; tragedy tends to be more concentrated and may achieve poetic effect better through music and spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epic, consider its capacity for simultaneous incidents and variety of episodes; when comparing, note differences in metre, unity, concentration of effect, and audience cultivation. Tragedy may be superior when it attains its specific poetic effect more powerfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Audience Effects and Didactic Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation pleases because people delight in representations and in learning; poetic pleasure derives partly from apprehending meaning and learning about character and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design works that enable spectators to 'learn' from imitation—recognition, discovery, and the emotional arc contribute to this pleasure. Consider audience cultivation: some effects require a more cultivated audience to appreciate subtler presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Critics' Objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics' objections to poetry fall into five kinds: (1) impossible, (2) improbable, (3) corrupting, (4) contradictory, (5) against technical correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the twelve kinds of solutions Aristotle catalogues (linguistic, probabilistic, metrical, traditional, poetic purpose, etc.) to answer such objections; determine whether the objection targets poetic ends or accidental matters.
